newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - July 1.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - July 1.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Tuesday:
* Communist China has now resumed sovereignty over Hong Kong, and the former British colony has responded in true fashion: It has found an opportunity to make money.
* Campbell Soup named Dale Morrison its next chief executive, succeeding David Johnson, who had started a reorganization of the company.

* Coca-Cola Co and a host of other stocks fell sharply in their final trade on the day, and some traders suggested the action was the result of end-of-quarter performance enhancement by fund managers.
* AT&T announced a cut in its long-distance calling rates for the first time in five years.
* GE Capital has agreed to acquire Colonial Penn P&C Group from Leucadia National Corp for $950 million.
* JP Foodservice has agreed to acquire Rykoff-Sexton for about $689 million in stock.
* U.S. President Bill Clinton issued a counter proposal of $135 billion in tax cuts over five years, seeking a compromise with the Republican-controlled Congress.
* Julian Robertson, the hedge-fund manager, is raising a new fund of as much as $1 billion and is mulling taking on a partner for his Tiger Management.
* NationsBank, confirming rumours that had been circulating in recent days, has agreed to acquire closely held investment bank Montgomery Securities for $1.2 billion.
* A left-wing German politician was acquitted by a court in Berlin of charges she aided and supported guerrilla acts with information linked to her home page on the Internet.

* Bantam Doubleday Dell, an American publishing subsidiary of Bertelsmann AG, has won a preliminary victory in Polish civil court to halt publication of a heavily edited version of its biography of Pope John Paul II.
* A group of doctors are calling for a moratorium on corporate takeovers of health services and for limits on the companies' intrusion into decisions made by physicians.
* The Dow Jones Industrials, surprising analysts and investors, actually gained 16.5 percent in the quarter that ended on Monday.
* The Federal Reserve is likely to hold interest rates at current levels, but the central bank could feel compelled to tighten monetary policy later in the year.
* Under pressure from a federal court judge's ruling temporarily blocking their proposed $4 billion combination, Office Depot Inc and Staples Inc executives said the merger is likely dead.
* American insurance companies are finding that they are increasingly being duped by policyholders who pretend they or their loved ones have died overseas.
